papers.title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29132v1

summary.one_liner: DeepDOSReasoner is a machine-learning model that predicts electronic and phonon density-of-states spectra directly from crystal structure, using source attention and a continuity-equation transport step that enforces nonnegativity and total-state conservation, and is evaluated on a prospective DFT-validated screen of new materials.
summary.plain: Researchers want to know how a material's energy levels are spread out, but computing this with a standard quantum simulation is slow, and many materials in a public database lack it. This paper describes a computer model that predicts these energy-level spectra from a material's atomic arrangement in a fraction of a second. The authors report it was more accurate than the methods they compared against, and that 25 of its top 50 picks for a particular band-gap property were confirmed by new simulations.
summary.why: Filling in missing spectra for tens of thousands of database entries could speed up searches for materials with useful electronic or thermal properties, such as for solar cells or electronics. The text reports the released predictions but does not show how they perform in real laboratory use, so practical impact remains to be tested.
summary.background:
- Density of states (DOS): a count of how many allowed energy levels exist at each energy; it governs how a material conducts electricity, absorbs light, and stores heat.
- Electronic DOS (eDOS) concerns electrons; phonon DOS (phDOS) concerns atomic vibrations.
- Density functional theory (DFT): a standard, costly quantum-mechanical calculation used to compute these spectra.
- Materials Project: a public database of computed material properties, many entries missing these spectra.
- Valence-band (VB) gap: an energy range with no allowed electron states in the valence band, relevant to electronic behavior.
- Conservation and nonnegativity: physical constraints that the predicted spectrum must add up to the correct total number of states and never go below zero.
- Ablation: a test where parts of a model are removed to see whether each part matters.

papers.abstract: Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.

papers.title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30066v1

summary.one_liner: The paper argues that standard reliability metrics for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) do not predict whether a reliability intervention improves DFT-based screening of crystal structures, and proposes decision-aligned evaluation instead.
summary.plain: Scientists use machine-learning models to quickly estimate which candidate materials are promising, so that only a few need costly quantum-mechanical checks. This paper asks whether making those models more "reliable" by standard measures actually leads to better choices about which candidates to check. The authors found that several common fixes can look successful on their own metric while leaving the final screening decision unchanged or worse.
summary.why: Materials discovery pipelines spend heavily on expensive simulations, so whether a model fix actually saves that cost matters in practice. The paper's central point, that accuracy or uncertainty scores are not the same as decision value, may also apply to other AI-guided screening tasks, though the text itself only covers materials.
summary.background:
- Interatomic potential: a fast machine-learned model that estimates the energy of an atomic arrangement, standing in for slower quantum calculations.
- DFT (density functional theory): the expensive quantum-mechanical calculation used to verify candidates.
- Convex hull / near-hull candidates: a crystal is stable if its energy lies on or near the lower envelope of energies for competing compositions; "near-hull" means close to stable.
- Recall: the fraction of truly promising candidates that the screening procedure correctly keeps.
- Calibration: whether a model's stated uncertainty matches how often it is actually wrong.
- Novelty detection: flagging inputs that differ from the training data, suggesting the model may be unreliable there.
- Foundation model: a large model pretrained broadly, then applied to many tasks.

papers.abstract: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.

papers.title: Unveiling the Complex high-pressure phases of Sodium at the Melting Curve Minimum via Data-Drive Crystal Structure Prediction
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29889v1

summary.background:
- Crystal structure: the repeating three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a solid; phases are different such arrangements of the same material.
- Melting curve: the line on a pressure-temperature plot showing where a solid melts; its minimum is where melting temperature is lowest.
- Enthalpy and Gibbs free energy: energy-like measures used to judge which structure is most stable at given pressure and temperature (the lower, the more favored).
- Crystal structure prediction: computer searches that generate and rank possible atomic arrangements without prior experimental structure.
- Deep Potential models: machine-learned interatomic potentials that approximate quantum-mechanical forces much faster than direct calculation; concurrent learning means the training set is expanded iteratively during the search.
- First-principles calculations: energy calculations from quantum mechanics without fitted parameters.
- Solid-liquid coexistence simulations: simulations that find the temperature at which solid and liquid are in equilibrium.
- Labels such as tI50 or oC120 denote crystal lattice type (tetragonal, orthorhombic, etc.) and the number of atoms in the unit cell.
summary.one_liner: Combines CALYPSO structure prediction with concurrent-learning Deep Potential models to search for candidate crystal structures of high-pressure sodium phases near its melting-curve minimum, and compares their enthalpy, Gibbs free energy, and solid-liquid coexistence behavior.
summary.plain: Sodium, a simple metal, forms many complicated crystal arrangements under pressure, and several of these observed in experiments have never had their atomic layouts worked out. The authors used computer searches over more than 1.6 million candidate configurations, guided by machine-learned interaction models, to propose atomic arrangements for these phases. They report that one known structure is recovered, and that several candidate structures are energetically close to one another and to established sodium phases near the melting minimum.
summary.why: Sodium's unusually many high-pressure phases are a known puzzle, and the paper offers specific structural models that experimentalists could test against measured diffraction data. The text reports that the candidates are close in stability and that the ranking depends on model accuracy, so the conclusions are provisional rather than settled.

papers.abstract: Sodium exhibits a remarkable concentration of complex crystalline phases near its melting-curve minimum, yet the atomic arrangements of several experimentally observed phases remain unresolved. Here, we combine CALYPSO crystal structure prediction with Deep Potential models developed through concurrent learning to explore this structural landscape. Searches over more than 1.6 million configurations recover the previously reported $I4/m$ structure of $tI50$ and identify candidate atomic arrangements for $oC120$ and $aP90$, together with three additional low-enthalpy structures, $tI52$, $oP72$, and $oP92$. The proposed candidates reproduce key features of the experimentally indexed cell geometries. First-principles enthalpy calculations, Gibbs free-energy comparisons, and solid--liquid coexistence simulations reveal close competition among these structures and established sodium phases. Near the calculated reference melting minimum, $tI50$ is favored over $cI16$ and $oP8$, whereas $oC120$ and $aP90$ remain closely competitive, with their relative stability sensitive to model accuracy. These results provide testable structural models for unresolved experimental phases and reveal multiple closely competing low-enthalpy configurations near sodium's melting minimum

papers.title: Defect Engineering of the Water-Carbon Interface: Insights from First-Principles Calculations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28201v1

summary.background:
- Solid-liquid interfaces: the boundary where a solid surface meets water, where chemical reactions happen.
- Hydrovoltaics: devices that generate electricity from water moving or evaporating across a material.
- First-principles calculations: simulations that compute material behavior directly from the laws of quantum physics, without fitted experimental inputs.
- Defects: imperfections in a material's atomic structure, such as missing atoms (vacancies), edges, or swapped-in foreign atoms (doping).
- Energy barrier: the energy hill a reaction must climb; lower barriers mean faster reactions.
- Gibbs free energy near zero for hydrogen evolution: a sign that a surface can bind and release hydrogen efficiently, which is favorable for making hydrogen.
- Dangling bonds: unpaired chemical bonds at a broken edge that tend to be chemically reactive.
- Charge transfer: movement of electrons between the material and water molecules, linked to electricity generation.
summary.one_liner: Using first-principles (quantum-mechanical, computer-based) calculations, this paper maps how topological, point, line, edge and doping defects in carbon materials change water-carbon interactions relevant to water splitting, evaporation-driven electricity, and catalysis.
summary.plain: Carbon materials that touch water are central to devices that turn evaporating water into electricity or split water to make hydrogen. Real carbon is full of small flaws, but how those flaws affect water has been poorly understood. The authors used computer simulations to test many kinds of flaws and reported how each one changes water splitting, charge transfer to evaporating water, and hydrogen formation.
summary.why: The text reports specific effects, such as edge defects lowering the water-dissociation energy barrier by up to 30 times and mono-vacancies boosting charge transfer by up to 12.4 times, which could guide the design of hydrovoltaic and catalytic devices. These are computed predictions from the abstract alone, so they still need experimental confirmation before any practical significance is clear.

papers.abstract: Interactions at solid-liquid interfaces are fundamental to hydrovoltaic and catalytic technologies. While carbon nanomaterials have been extensively studied, the role of abundant defects in amorphous carbon remains poorly understood. Here, using first-principles calculations, we systematically investigate how various defects (topological, point, line, edge, and doping defects) modulate water-carbon interactions. We find that armchair-edge defects with dangling bonds reduce the energy barrier for water dissociation by up to 30 times compared with pristine carbon, while di-vacancies exhibit a near-zero Gibbs free energy for hydrogen evolution, enabling potential hydrogen evolution reaction activity on a purely carbon-based interface. Moreover, mono-vacancy defects, characterized by reduced electronic localization, enhance charge transfer to evaporating water molecules by up to 12.4 times, a key factor in evaporation-induced electricity generation. Crucially, we demonstrate that coupling distinct defects produces synergistic effects that outperform individual defects, revealing a promising strategy for designing multifunctional interfaces. These insights establish a defect-engineering framework for the rational design of high-efficiency hydrovoltaic and catalytic devices.

papers.title: Designing Perovskites for Chemical Looping Hydrogen Production
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27580v1

summary.background:
- Perovskites: a family of crystal materials with a flexible structure whose elements can be swapped (A and B sites) to tune properties.
- Chemical looping: a cycle in which a solid material is reduced and then re-oxidized, here used to produce hydrogen from steam.
- Hydrogen production capacity (HPC): the amount of hydrogen produced per gram of material, in mmol per gram.
- Active learning: a loop where a model picks the next most informative experiments or calculations, then updates itself.
- Autoencoder: a neural network that compresses data into a smaller set of numbers and reconstructs it; the Wasserstein variant is a specific training method.
- Deep ensemble: many neural networks trained together whose spread gives a sense of uncertainty.
- Multi-objective ranking: choosing candidates by balancing several criteria at once, such as performance, cost and environmental impact.
summary.one_liner: An autonomous active-learning loop (Wasserstein autoencoder plus deep-ensemble surrogate) searched perovskite compositions for hydrogen production capacity in chemical looping, and then ranked 20 candidates by cost, supply resilience and environmental/health impact.
summary.plain: Researchers wanted to find better solid materials for making hydrogen in a cyclic chemical process, where a metal-oxide-like material repeatedly gives up and takes back oxygen. There are too many possible mixtures of elements to test one by one, so they used a computer program that proposes new mixtures, learns from the results, and repeats. Over 50 cycles, the average hydrogen yield of the proposed materials rose from 0.41 to 2.05 mmol per gram, and the best reached about 2.65 to 2.99.
summary.why: It shows a way to speed up materials searches while also weighing price, supply and safety, which matters for practical deployment of cleaner hydrogen. The text does not report experimental validation or how far these computed values would hold up in a real reactor, so its practical impact is still uncertain.

papers.abstract: Perovskites are promising materials for chemical looping hydrogen production (CLHP) due to their compositional flexibility and tunable redox properties. However, cation substitution opens a vast compositional space, making screening for new high-performing materials computationally demanding. Here, an autonomous active-learning framework combining a Wasserstein autoencoder (WAE) with a deep ensemble surrogate model was used to search for perovskites with a high hydrogen production capacity (HPC). In seven independent runs of 50 cycles, the mean HPC of the acquired compositions rose from 0.41 mmol H$_2$ g$^{-1}$ in the starting set to 2.05 mmol H$_2$ g$^{-1}$, and the best compositions reached 2.65-2.99 mmol H$_2$ g$^{-1}$. All runs enriched Sn on the B-site, mostly combined with Ti and with Mg, Ce, K and Y on the A-site. Twenty diverse candidates (2.22-2.84 mmol H$_2$ g$^{-1}$) were then selected by a multi-objective ranking that also accounts for raw-material price, supply resilience and potential environmental and health impacts. The approach links materials discovery with practical deployment constraints, and the methodology is transferable to other chemical looping processes.

papers.title: Edge-dislocation interactions with sub 3 nm vacancy and interstitial clusters in FeCr alloys: Mechanisms, Obstacle strength and Fate
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27583v1

summary.background:
- Edge dislocation: a line defect in a crystal; its glide through the lattice is what makes metals deform.
- Obstacle strength: how hard a defect resists a passing dislocation; here reported in MPa and as a dimensionless alpha in hardening models.
- Vacancy / interstitial cluster: small groups of missing atoms or extra atoms in a crystal lattice, typically a few nanometres across.
- Dispersed-barrier hardening: a standard model where hardening scales with the square root of defect density times defect strength.
- Molecular dynamics (MD): simulating how atoms move according to interatomic forces, limited to very short timescales and small sample sizes.
- Fe-Cr alloys: iron with 3-10% chromium, a model for reactor structural steels.
- TEM (transmission electron microscopy): imaging technique that resolves defects only above a certain size.
summary.one_liner: Molecular dynamics simulations of an edge dislocation passing through sub-3 nm vacancy and mixed Fe-Cr interstitial clusters in Fe-3Cr, Fe-5Cr and Fe-10Cr at 300 K, quantifying obstacle strength, survival, and the dispersed-barrier alpha values implied for low-dose hardening.
summary.plain: Metal alloys used in nuclear reactors get harder and more brittle under radiation, even at doses where microscopes show no visible damage. This paper uses computer simulations of atoms to study tiny clusters of missing or extra atoms, too small to see under a microscope, and how strongly they block the movement of dislocations (line-like defects whose motion makes metals soft). The authors find that vacancy clusters (missing atoms) are strong blockers that always survive, while most interstitial clusters (extra atoms) are weaker and usually get absorbed.
summary.why: Models of radiation hardening are usually fitted to defects visible in electron microscopes, so they may overstate how strong those visible defects are if invisible clusters contribute. The paper argues that earlier fitted strength values are inflated for this reason, which could matter for predicting the lifetime of reactor steels; the link to real materials is inferred from simulations and has not been tested here.

papers.abstract: Fe-Cr alloys harden at irradiation doses where transmission electron microscopy (TEM) shows no defects, implicating defects too small to be resolved. Their obstacle strength is unknown, so hardening models ignore them and fit measured hardening to visible defects alone. Here, molecular dynamics drives an edge dislocation through relaxed 1-3 nm vacancy and mixed Fe-Cr interstitial clusters in Fe-3Cr, Fe-5Cr and Fe-10Cr at 300 K. Vacancy clusters relax into platelets whose strength rises with size to about 350 MPa at 2.9 nm, following strong-obstacle scaling independently of Cr content, and always survive dislocation passage. Interstitial clusters relax into $\frac{1}{2}\langle 111 \rangle$, mixed or $\langle 100 \rangle$ loops. They are mostly weaker than platelets of the same size, their strength varies up to fivefold with the local Cr arrangement, and most are absorbed. Only $\langle 100 \rangle$ loops in Fe-5Cr and Fe-10Cr often survive. During pinning, Cr collects at the junction between these loops and the dislocation; atom tracking for one loop shows that more than half comes from the loop itself. Surviving loops are not stronger than absorbed ones: strength and survival are thus distinct. Computed dispersed-barrier strengths ($\alpha \approx$ 0.02-0.25) are upper bounds that lie below the $\alpha$ values obtained in earlier studies by fitting hardening to TEM-visible loops. These earlier values are therefore inflated by TEM-invisible defects. Wherever small vacancy clusters form, they are more effective obstacles than interstitial clusters of the same size. These defect-specific strengths and fates provide a physical basis for models of low-dose hardening.

papers.title: Growth and anisotropic directional dependent transport properties of Altermagnetic CrSb
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27072v1

summary.background:
- Antiferromagnet: a material whose neighboring magnetic moments point in opposite directions, so it has little net magnetism.
- Altermagnet: a newer class of antiferromagnet whose electron spin splitting depends on the direction of motion, which can be exploited in spintronics.
- Spintronics: electronics that use the spin of electrons as well as their charge.
- Single crystal grown by flux or vapor transport: a method of growing a large, well-ordered crystal from a molten metal bath (flux) or from a gas that deposits solid material.
- Magnetoresistance: the change in a material's electrical resistance when a magnetic field is applied.
- Hall effect: a sideways voltage produced when current flows through a material in a magnetic field; its sign reveals the type of charge carriers.
- Residual resistivity ratio: a rough gauge of crystal purity and defect level; higher values usually mean fewer defects.
summary.one_liner: A comparison of CrSb altermagnet single crystals grown by Sb-self flux, Bi flux, and chemical vapor transport, examining structure, magnetization, and anisotropic magnetotransport across growth routes.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a metal called CrSb, which is magnetically ordered in a special way that may be useful for future electronics. The authors grew crystals of it using three different recipes and then compared their shapes, magnetic behavior, and how electricity flows through them in different directions. They found the crystals behave broadly alike, but the Bi-flux crystals scatter electric carriers more strongly and show much weaker magnetoresistance.
summary.why: Crystal growth method can change the measured electrical properties of a material, so this comparison helps researchers pick suitable samples for spintronics work, which aims to use electron spin in devices. The text does not report device results, so its link to practical applications is only a suggestion.

papers.abstract: CrSb is a metallic altermagnet exhibiting large momentum-dependent spin splitting and antifer- romagnetic ordering well above room temperature. Although its electronic and magnetotransport properties have attracted considerable attention, a systematic comparison of crystals prepared us- ing different growth methods remains limited. Here we investigate the structural, magnetic, and anisotropic transport properties of CrSb single crystals grown by Sb(self)-flux, Bi flux, and chem- ical vapor transport (CVT). Each of these growth reveals distinct crystal morphologies. Magne- tization measurements exhibit broadly consistent antiferromagnetic responses, with an additional low-temperature contribution observed in Bi-flux-grown crystals. All samples display metallic resis- tivity and positive, nonsaturating magnetoresistance up to 9 T. Sb-flux- and CVT-grown crystals exhibit comparable residual resistivity ratios and magnetoresistance, whereas Bi-flux-grown crys- tals show enhanced residual resistivity and a substantially reduced magnetoresistance, consistent with stronger carrier scattering. Hall measurements reveal a pronounced dependence on the field- current configuration, including nonlinear field dependence and opposite Hall polarities for different crystallographic orientations. These results establish the reproducibility of anisotropic magneto- transport across distinct growth routes while highlighting the sensitivity of carrier scattering to crystal-growth conditions. Our findings provide a comparative framework for selecting CrSb single crystals for orientation-dependent transport and spintronic investigations.

papers.title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26186v1

summary.background:
- Electronic flat band: an energy band that is nearly horizontal, so electrons in it have very similar energies regardless of their momentum; such bands are of interest for strongly correlated electronic behavior.
- Bandwidth score: a single number summarizing how spread out a band is; a smaller number means flatter.
- Reward misalignment: when the score an AI system is optimized for does not match what people actually want.
- Pairwise comparison: asking an expert which of two options they prefer, then inferring a overall preference scale from many such choices.
- Crystal diffusion model: a generative model that proposes atomic crystal structures by iteratively refining random arrangements.
- Synthesizability and phonon properties: whether a material can plausibly be made, and how its atoms vibrate, both mentioned as extensions.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that disagreements between a fixed numerical reward and expert judgment can point to promising materials, using electronic flat bands as the test case and learning expert preferences to steer a crystal diffusion model.
summary.plain: Computer models that design new materials are usually scored by a fixed rule, and this paper asks what happens when that rule disagrees with human experts. The authors ask experts to compare pairs of candidate materials, learn their preferences from those comparisons, and use them to guide a generative model. They report that experts mostly agree with the numerical score on the flattest electronic bands but disagree systematically elsewhere, and that the learned preferences favor some reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would have discarded.
summary.why: It reframes a mismatch between AI objectives and expert judgment as a possible source of new candidates rather than only a failure, which may matter for AI-guided materials search. The text does not show that the flagged materials have been synthesized or validated beyond the stated comparisons, so the practical payoff is still unclear.

papers.abstract: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.

papers.title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25779v1

summary.background:
- Thermoreflectance: a non-contact optical method that uses a laser pulse to heat a surface and a second beam to detect small changes in reflected light, revealing how fast heat spreads.
- Thermal conductivity: how readily a material conducts heat.
- Interface conductance: how easily heat passes across a boundary between two materials; a bottleneck in many devices.
- Specific heat: how much heat a material stores per unit of temperature change.
- Wide-field vs. scanning imaging: capturing a whole area at once versus building a map point by point.
- Subsurface characterization: probing structure beneath the surface without cutting or destroying the sample.
- Machine learning / AI-agentic design: algorithms that learn from data, and systems that propose and run experiments with limited human direction.
summary.one_liner: A review of how artificial intelligence is being applied to pump-probe thermoreflectance imaging for mapping thermal properties, interfacial heat transport, and subsurface structure in nanoscale materials and devices.
summary.plain: This is a review article about using artificial intelligence to make heat-flow measurements of very small materials and electronic devices faster and more informative. The authors describe recent work that uses AI to process large volumes of thermal images, to visualize how heat crosses boundaries between materials, and to look beneath surfaces without damaging them. They also outline possible next steps, such as mapping which heat-carrying vibrations dominate, building three-dimensional property maps, and using AI to plan experiments.
summary.why: As devices and materials shrink and become more varied internally, heat behaves differently at local defects and interfaces, so fast, accurate thermal mapping matters for electronics and materials design. The text is a general overview and does not report new experimental results, so its practical impact is best judged by the specific studies it surveys.

papers.abstract: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing. As critical dimensions and architectures of novel materials and high performance electronics shrink and become more heterogeneous, thermal transport is no longer governed by bulk material properties alone, but by local variations in microstructure, such as interfaces and defects, while the operating conditions can also play a role. With the development of non-contact pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and interface conductance can be mapped either through wide-field thermos-reflectance images or by scanning technique. However, key challenges remain such as the balance between imaging throughput and measurement accuracy, the extraction of multiple parameters with high confidence, and non-intrusive subsurface characterization, etc. This Review highlights recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI)-assistance in high-throughput data processing, visualizing interfacial thermal transport, and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, and offers outlooks for future research directions such as spectral mapping of heat carriers, three-dimensional property mapping, and AI-agentic experimental designs. We anticipate this Review will motivate future efforts in combining AI with experimental techniques to achieve unprecedented capabilities for thermal characterization of nanoscale materials and device characterization, facilitating materials discovery and electronics revolution.

papers.title: Physics-Guided Crystal Structure Elucidation from Powder X-Ray Diffraction with Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23760v1

summary.background:
- Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD): shining X-rays on a powdered sample produces a pattern of peaks whose positions and heights reflect the arrangement of atoms in the crystal.
- Crystal structure: the repeating 3D arrangement of atoms in a solid, described by a unit cell (box size and angles) and a space group (its symmetry).
- Wyckoff sites: the symmetry-defined positions atoms can occupy within a space group.
- Structure prediction / evolutionary search: generating many candidate arrangements, keeping and mutating the better ones, much like natural selection.
- Machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP): a trained model that estimates the energy of an atomic arrangement quickly, standing in for slower quantum calculations.
- Convex hull / meV per atom: a measure of whether a structure is stable relative to competing phases; energies are small energy differences per atom (meV = thousandths of an electron-volt).
- DFT (density functional theory): a standard quantum-mechanical calculation used here as a more accurate check.
- ICSD (Inorganic Crystal Structure Database): a catalogue of known experimentally determined inorganic structures, used to test whether candidates are new.
summary.one_liner: XCAPE is a symmetry-aware evolutionary crystal structure prediction framework that uses experimental powder X-ray diffraction data, composition, cell parameters and space group, with a universal machine-learning interatomic potential to speed up relaxations, to propose atomic structures for unresolved materials.
summary.plain: Researchers often shoot X-rays at a powdered sample and get a pattern of peaks, but turning that pattern back into exact atom positions is often ambiguous. This paper describes a computer method that combines the measured pattern with known chemistry and symmetry, then searches for atomic arrangements that are both energetically reasonable and match the pattern. The authors report that it recovered most of a set of known benchmark structures and proposed 12 new candidate structures that do not appear in a standard crystal database.

papers.abstract: Determining unique atomic coordinates from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) remains challenging because peak overlap, weak scattering from light elements, limited scattering contrast between elements with similar atomic numbers, and experimental noise render the inverse problem underdetermined. Here, we present XCAPE (XRD-Constrained Accelerated Prediction Engine), a crystal structure prediction (CSP) framework that integrates experimentally derived composition, unit cell parameters, space group, and PXRD data into a symmetry-aware evolutionary search. XCAPE explores Wyckoff-site configurations using tailored mutation operations, evaluates candidates by both energetic stability and diffraction agreement, and accelerates geometry optimization using a universal machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The framework recovered 71 of 77 database-derived benchmark structures (92.2%) from simulated PXRD patterns and all 12 reference structures from experimental PXRD patterns. It further identified 12 candidate structure assignments that are consistent with experimental PXRD patterns, lack matching entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), and are thermodynamically competitive at the MLIP level. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations showed that 10 of these 12 candidates lie within 10 meV/atom of the convex hull. By bridging experimental diffraction data and physically plausible atomistic models, XCAPE can provide structural insight into previously unresolved materials and support accelerated materials discovery in automated research workflows.

papers.title: Materials representations organize transferable supervision for chemical extrapolation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23837v1

summary.background:
- Machine-learning property prediction: models learn from labeled examples (for example, measured or computed formation energies and bandgaps) and predict values for new compounds.
- Chemical extrapolation: predicting for compounds containing elements that do not appear in the training data.
- Engineered descriptors: hand-designed numerical features describing a compound from elemental properties (such as electronegativity).
- Crystal-graph encoder: a neural network that represents a crystal structure as a graph of atoms and bonds and learns a numerical representation of it, here pretrained on other data.
- Formation energy and bandgap: standard materials properties; errors are reported in meV per atom (thousandths of an electron-volt) and meV.
- Periodic groups: columns of the periodic table, a simple chemical grouping used as a baseline.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that materials representations can rank chemical elements by how much transferable training supervision their compounds provide for predicting properties of compounds containing unseen elements, without target labels, with a pretrained crystal-graph encoder outperforming engineered descriptors and periodic-table groupings.
summary.plain: Machine-learning models that predict material properties often have to make guesses about compounds built from chemical elements they never saw in training. This paper asks which compounds made of other elements actually help with such guesses. The authors found that a pretrained neural encoder ranks elements by how useful their compounds are, and removing the compounds of its top-ranked elements from training hurt prediction accuracy far more than removing those of lower-ranked elements.
summary.why: Choosing which data to label or collect is expensive in materials discovery, so a ranking that can be computed before training could guide dataset assessment and label acquisition. The text reports consistency across properties, regressors and datasets, but it is a single preprint-style abstract, so how far the result generalizes beyond the tested settings is not established here.

papers.abstract: Materials discovery often requires chemical extrapolation beyond labeled data. When target compounds contain elements absent from training, which compounds of other elements provide transferable supervision remains unclear. Here we show that, without target-property labels, materials representations rank other elements by the supervision their compounds provide. Engineered descriptors rank them largely by elemental-property similarity, whereas a pretrained crystal-graph encoder ranks them by the geometry of its learned representation. At fixed training-set size, excluding the compounds of the encoder's six top-ranked elements raises formation-energy and bandgap errors by 100-110 meV per atom and 42-85 meV, versus little change for six lower-ranked elements. The rankings hold across properties, regressors and datasets. The encoder's ranking outperforms elemental-property similarity and periodic groups, suggesting that it captures how elements behave within compounds. Materials representations thus organize transferable supervision, which can be identified before model training, informing dataset assessment and label acquisition.

papers.title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22050v1

summary.background:
- Crystal structure prediction: working out the 3D arrangement of atoms in a crystal from its chemical makeup.
- Diffusion model: a generative AI method that learns to turn random noise into structured data by reversing a gradual noising process.
- Match Rate: the fraction of generated structures that match a known reference structure.
- RMSE (root-mean-square error): a measure of how far predicted atom positions are from the true ones; lower is better.
- Generation bias: systematic unevenness in how well a model performs across different data types.
- Benchmark datasets: standard test collections, such as Carbon-24, used to compare methods.
summary.one_liner: DSADiff is a diffusion model for crystal structure prediction that uses a layered analysis (LAS) to identify crystal complexity and elemental imbalance as sources of generation bias, then feeds these factors into a unified difficulty representation that guides both feature modeling and training.
summary.plain: Predicting how atoms arrange themselves in a crystal is a key step in finding new materials, and AI models that do this often work well on some kinds of materials but poorly on others. This paper looks for the reasons behind that uneven performance and finds two likely causes: how structurally complex a crystal is, and how unevenly its chemical elements are represented in the training data. The authors then build a model that takes these two factors into account so it learns more evenly across different kinds of samples.
summary.why: Reducing bias in generative models could matter for materials discovery, where models that fail on certain material types give misleading results. The text reports that the approach improves Match Rate and RMSE on three benchmarks, with a maximum Match Rate gain of 9% and claims of new state-of-the-art results; the broader significance beyond these benchmarks is not established in the text.

papers.abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.

papers.title: Weight-Space Programming for Materials Science
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22013v1

summary.background:
- Spearman correlation: a score from -1 to 1 for how well a ranking matches the true order; higher is better.
- Weights: the adjustable numbers inside a neural network that set how it turns inputs into predictions.
- Hidden units: the intermediate computing nodes of a small network between inputs and outputs.
- Gaussian process: a statistical model that gives predictions with uncertainty and can use a prior mean as its starting guess.
- Bayesian optimization: a strategy for choosing which experiment to run next, aiming to find a good result in few tries; "regret" measures how far the chosen results fall short of the best possible.
- Bayesian neural network: a neural network that expresses uncertainty about its outputs.
- Phase-equilibrium targets: properties describing which phases of an alloy are stable at given conditions, here computed with Thermo-Calc software.
- Generative discovery loops: cycles where a model proposes new crystal structures, which are then evaluated and fed back.
- Weight-space programming: the idea, from prior work, of having a language model write network weights directly as text.
summary.one_liner: A general-purpose language model writes all the weights of a small neural network as text, using only a task description and input names, and the resulting networks serve as zero-label priors for ranking materials, Gaussian-process and Bayesian-optimization surrogates, and screening generated crystals.
summary.plain: Materials scientists often start a search with almost no measured data, so their predictive models have little to learn from. This paper asks a language model to write out the numbers (weights) of a small network from its general knowledge of materials, given only a plain-words task description and the input names. The reported result is that these written-out networks rank candidate materials reasonably well before any labels are collected, and they help as a starting point once a few labels are added.
summary.why: Early-stage materials searches are expensive and data-poor, so a useful zero-label starting model could cut wasted experiments. The paper reports gains mainly in the first few tens of labels and only for targets that simple rules or sub-system extrapolation do not already capture, so its value is narrower than the headline numbers alone suggest.

papers.abstract: A materials discovery campaign often begins with almost no measurements of the property it is searching for, and the models that rank candidates or screen the output of a generator then have to be built from those first few labels. Following recent work on weight-space programming, in which a language model writes the weights of a small network directly as text, we show that a general-purpose model, given the task in words, the names of the inputs and a network of 16 hidden units with every weight set to zero, can provide this starting point by filling in all of the weights from what it has learned about materials. With no labels, the networks of the strongest model rank experimental alloys at Spearman co-efficient = 0.64 to 0.79, where the best of five simple descriptors reaches 0.47 to 0.62. They rank the bulk modulus of crystals added during generative discovery loops at 0.95, where the inverse volume per atom reaches 0.89, and 35 phase-equilibrium targets computed with Thermo-Calc at a mean of 0.67, close to the 0.70 of an extrapolation from calculated binary and ternary data. As the prior mean of a Gaussian process they raise the ranking at five labels from 0.35 to 0.69 on alloys and from 0.15 to 0.95 on crystals, and they lower the regret of Bayesian optimization significantly on 4 of 5 experimental tasks and on 13 to 16 of 33 computed targets, depending on how multiple tests are corrected, without raising it significantly on any. The same networks also serve as the mean of a Bayesian neural network and as a screen for the samples of two crystal generators, where they do as well as standard models trained on 400 labeled structures. The gain is confined to the first tens of labels and to targets that no rule or sub-system extrapolation already ranks.

papers.title: Crystal Structure Prediction from Search to Learning: A 30-Year Expedition
papers.label: arXiv:2611.17670v1

summary.background:
- Crystal: a solid whose atoms repeat in a regular 3D pattern.
- Crystal structure prediction: computing the likely repeating pattern from chemical composition alone.
- Energy landscape: the map of how stable each possible arrangement is; the most stable one is usually the one seen in nature.
- First-principles calculation: physics-based quantum calculations, with no fitting to experimental data.
- Deep generative model: a machine-learning model (such as diffusion or flow models) that proposes new candidate structures.
- Benchmark / leaderboard: a shared set of test targets used to compare methods, here reported as top-1 recovery (whether the correct structure is ranked first).
- Diffraction or microscopy: experimental techniques used to confirm a crystal's atomic arrangement.
summary.one_liner: A survey of 30 years of crystal structure prediction (CSP) methods, software, and benchmarks, classifying search and learning approaches and auditing predictions against experimentally confirmed materials.
summary.plain: This paper reviews three decades of work on predicting how atoms or molecules will arrange themselves into a crystal, given only the chemical recipe and conditions like pressure. The authors sort the many computer methods into families, such as trial-and-error searches, evolutionary searches, and newer machine-learning generators. They report that no single approach clearly wins on benchmarks, and that most of the 68 audited materials with predicted structures were predicted before experiments, mostly by first-principles search rather than deep generative models.
summary.why: Predicting crystal structures before synthesis could help guide the search for new materials for batteries, electronics, or pharmaceuticals, so the field's track record matters to those who fund and use it. The text's most specific finding is that, within the reviewed evidence, no confirmed discovery was made by a deep generative model ahead of experiment, which tempers claims about AI-driven materials discovery.

papers.abstract: Crystal structure prediction (CSP) determines periodic atomic or molecular arrangements from chemical composition and physical conditions. Over three decades, CSP has evolved from chemical construction and global energy optimization to hybrid approaches combining symmetry, learned potentials, adaptive search, and deep generative models. This survey reviews method, software, review, and benchmark records from 1996 to October 2026, covering inorganic and molecular crystals, including formula-conditioned diffusion, flow, and autoregressive models that preserve composition. We classify methods by candidate construction and exploration: template and discrete construction, random search, evolutionary search, swarm and differential evolution, energy-landscape exploration, adaptive machine-learning-guided search, and learned generation. We distinguish representation, relaxation, ranking, and physical qualification. Benchmarks reveal no universally dominant approach. In a 46-target leaderboard snapshot, the best-performing template method achieves higher top-1 recovery than leading generative models, but paired tests show no statistically significant differences from several generative competitors. We also audit predictions for 68 experimentally examined materials, including 52 with structures confirmed by diffraction or microscopy. Predictions for 23 of the 68 preceded experiment, mostly through first-principles global search. Within the reviewed evidence, we find no independently confirmed discovery in which a deep generative model predicted the structure before experiment. We conclude with the principal limitations of current CSP algorithms and priorities for future research.

papers.title: A Machine-learning-aided Workflow for Sampling Small Polaron Dynamics in Energy Materials
papers.label: arXiv:2611.18041v1

summary.background:
- Conductivity: how easily electric charge moves through a material, measured in siemens per cm (S/cm).
- Small polaron: an electron or hole that is trapped by distorting the atoms around it, so it moves by hopping between sites.
- Density functional theory (DFT): a quantum-mechanical computational method for estimating material energies and structures; hybrid and self-interaction corrected variants are more accurate for trapped charges.
- Energy barrier: the energy needed for a polaron to hop from one site to the next; it sets how fast hopping happens.
- Machine-learning surrogate: a fast statistical model trained on expensive calculations to predict their results for new cases.
- Kinetic model: equations that combine hopping rates into an overall transport property.
- Li4Ti5O12 (LTO): a lithium-ion battery anode material.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses machine-learning surrogate models trained on density functional theory (DFT) calculations to sample small-polaron hopping barriers in the battery anode material Li4Ti5O12 (LTO), feeding them into a kinetic model to estimate room-temperature conductivity.
summary.plain: Many battery and solar materials conduct electricity because electrons or holes get trapped in a local distortion of the surrounding atoms, forming a "small polaron" that hops from site to site. Simulating every possible trapped state and hop is too expensive, so the authors trained a machine-learning model on a smaller set of quantum calculations to predict the rest. They used the results in a kinetic model to estimate how well lithium titanate (LTO), a battery anode material, conducts at room temperature.
summary.why: Estimating charge transport in realistic, defective materials from first principles is hard, and this work reports a predicted conductivity that the authors say falls within the experimental range, using 154 explicit calculations out of 3649 inequivalent barriers. The approach may be useful for other energy materials, but the text does not show how well it generalises beyond LTO.

papers.abstract: One of the defining characteristics of most energy materials, used as e.g.~battery electrodes, photovoltaics, or photocatalysts, is their ability conduct charges such as electrons and holes. The exact mechanism of this conductivity depends on the material, but is often dominated by the existence of mobile small polarons, i.e.~electrons or holes strongly localised through the polarisation of their environment. Computationally, small polarons can be treated with reasonably accuracy through the use of self-interaction corrected or hybrid density functional theory (DFT) together with local geometry optimisation. Similar approaches can be employed to determine the energy barriers to movement of the polarons through hopping. Unfortunately, realistic energy materials tend have very large numbers of symmetry inequivalent polaronic configurations and correspondingly large numbers of hopping barriers, making them hard to tackle explicitly. In this work we therefore extend the computational reach of DFT calculations with machine-learned (ML) surrogate models, which then feed into a kinetic model to quantitatively estimate the conductivity of a battery anode material (Li$_4$Ti$_5$O$_12$ or LTO) at realistic, defected conditions. We calculate the conductivity at room temperature to be 6.7 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ S/cm which lies well in the experimental range. To this end, we only needed a total of 154 polaron barrier calculations, out of 3649 symmetry inequivalent ones, achieving an over 20-fold increase of computational efficiency. Overall, our work demonstrates how DFT-trained ML surrogates can be used to quantitatively and efficiently sample the dynamics of small polarons in energy materials.
